tools.name: next_move
tools.description: The single highest-priority credit action right now: which card, how much, and by which date. Dated to the statement CLOSING date rather than the payment due date, because the closing balance is what Canadian issuers report to the bureaus. Use this when someone asks what to pay, what to do first, or

tools.name: reported_snapshot
tools.description: Per card: the balance in line to be reported at the next statement close, utilization, days left to change it, and the payment that would bring the card to target before it closes. tools.name: statement_calendar
tools.description: The upcoming dates that matter, in order: when to pay, when each statement closes (the bureau read), and when each payment is due (the delinquency line). Use it when someone asks about timing, what is coming up, or why the closing date differs from the due date.

tools.name: simulate_paydown
tools.description: What-if for a specific payment: pay this amount on this card before it closes, and here is the reported utilization before and after, per card and blended, plus a bounded modelled range. Use it when someone asks what happens if they pay a particular amount, or wants to compare two amounts.

tools.name: purchase_impact
tools.description: Before a large purchase: which card reports the least damage, which is cheapest to carry, and the trade-off when those are different cards. Returns both answers rather than one, because the card the bureaus notice least is often not the card with the lowest rate. Use it when someone asks which card

tools.name: credit_plan
tools.description: An ordered plan for one of three goals: raise_score, pay_down_balances, or build_credit. Safety steps come first (anything overdue, then imminent minimums), then goal steps, each with the specific action, the mechanism behind it, and a date. Use it when someone wants more than the next single action

tools.name: payoff_timeline
tools.description: How long a card takes to clear at a fixed monthly payment, and what the interest costs over that time. tools.name: close_card_impact
tools.description: Answers "should I cancel the credit card I never use", "is it bad to close a card", and any question about cancelling, downgrading, or consolidating cards. tools.name: newcomer_credit_path
tools.description: The ordered path for someone new to Canada: what to do before a SIN arrives, whether their home-country history can be imported and at which banks, how to get a first tradeline, and what accumulates after that. tools.name: credit_product_landscape
tools.description: Secured cards, credit-builder loans, and rebuild products available in Canada, grouped by how established they are, with which bureau each reports to. Single-bureau reporting is the detail most often missed: several well-known products report to Equifax only, which leaves the TransUnion file empty.

tools.name: about_credit_gps
tools.description: What this server is, what it deliberately does not do, and where its limits are. Call it when someone asks what Credit GPS is, who made this, whether their data is stored, or why an answer stopped short.

tools.name: find_statement_close_date
tools.description: How to find the statement closing date for a Canadian credit card — the date every other tool here depends on, and the one most people have never been shown. Give a payment due date and it also derives an estimate, because federally regulated issuers must allow at least a 21-day interest-free grace

tools.name: when_issuers_report
tools.description: How the monthly reporting cadence works in Canada, how long a change takes to appear on a file, and why an Equifax file and a TransUnion file for the same person differ. tools.name: missed_payment_guide
tools.description: What happens when a Canadian credit card payment is missed: the roughly 30-day gap before it is reported at all, the Canadian R1-R9 rating scale a tradeline actually carries, and how long a reported late payment stays on the file. tools.description: Retention periods on a Canadian credit file: closed accounts, late payments, collections, hard inquiries, bankruptcy, consumer proposals, judgments. Several differ from the American figures that dominate general knowledge — six years rather than seven for a late payment, three years rather than two

findings.title: Description issues instructions to the model
findings.detail: Description of "canadian_credit_mechanics" contains imperative instructions directed at the AI assistant rather than describing the tool. This is the core tool-poisoning technique.

evidence.snippet: Canada-specific mechanics of credit reporting, each entry leading with the correction to the common United States-based answer: the 300-900 scale and two-bureau…

findings.remediation: Treat the server as untrusted; the model may obey embedded instructions.
